summary: Specifies how a WebRTC data channel can carry real-time text conversation using the ITU-T T.140 format, and how SDP offer/answer negotiates it. This allows live text chat character by character in WebRTC calls. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes people want to type to each other live, letter by letter, as if talking. This document explains how to send that typing through a WebRTC call's message lane.

questions: how to send real-time text over webrtc
what is a t140 data channel
what is the default cps for t140
subtitle: Live, character-by-character text conversation carried over a WebRTC data channel and negotiated with SDP.

tldr.problem: People who type to each other live, as real-time text, need a transport inside WebRTC calls. The existing IP transport for T.140 is RTP-based, but WebRTC offers data channels.
tldr.mechanism: A T.140 data channel is a reliable, in-order WebRTC data channel with subprotocol t140, negotiated using SDP offer/answer attributes dcmap and dcsa. Text travels as T140blocks over SCTP.
tldr.outcome: Real-time text can be used alongside audio and video in WebRTC, with a character-rate limit, language and direction negotiated in SDP, and guidance for gateways to RTP-based text. It also updates RFC 8373.

today: RFC 8865 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It is not obsoleted or updated by a later RFC in the unit metadata, and it updates RFC 8373.

sections.title: Real-Time Text over Data Channels
sections.content:
T.140 is the ITU-T protocol for text conversation, also called real-time text. On IP networks its usual transport is the RTP payload for text conversation (RFC 4103). RFC 8865 specifies how a WebRTC data channel (RFC 8831) can be used instead, and how SDP offer/answer for data channels (RFC 8864) negotiates it.

A T.140 data channel is a data channel whose subprotocol is t140 and which is negotiated with SDP offer/answer. The use case is real-time text chat during an audio or video call. Text is typed by a person, so the rate is usually a few characters per second or less.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending a finished message, you send each letter as you type it. This document says how to do that inside a video call's side channel.

sections.title: Data Channel Properties
sections.content:
A T.140 data channel uses subprotocol identifier t140, reliable transmission and in-order delivery. The label is set as described in the SDP rules.

T.140 needs text delivered without duplication and in the original order. Over RTP this is achieved with sequence numbers to detect loss and a redundancy mechanism. A data channel already provides reliable, in-order delivery, so no redundancy or application-level loss detection is needed, and its latency is regarded as sufficient for T.140.
sections.plainLanguage: The side channel already promises that every letter arrives once and in order, so no extra safety copies are needed.

sections.title: Negotiating with SDP
sections.content:
The channel is described in the SDP media description for the SCTP association. Offerer and answerer MUST include a dcmap attribute with subprotocol="t140", and MAY include priority and label. They MUST NOT include max-retr or max-time; an answerer MUST reject an offer that has either. If ordered appears, it MUST be true.

Channel-specific attributes go inside dcsa attributes:

  • Character rate: fmtp with format t140 and a cps value, the maximum rate the endpoint can receive, as a mean in characters per second over any 10-second interval. The default is 30.
  • Language: hlang-send and hlang-recv from RFC 8373, with modality "written".
  • Direction: sendrecv, sendonly, recvonly or inactive. A data channel is always bidirectional, so these only limit which way text may be sent. Absent a marking, sendrecv applies.

Direction answers follow the usual pairing: a sendonly offer must be answered recvonly or inactive, a recvonly offer must be answered sendonly or inactive, and an inactive offer must be answered inactive. If a receiver gets text faster than it can handle, it SHOULD either signal it does not want more text or use flow control, though in applications such as emergency services it may be better to discard the overflow and insert a mark for loss.
sections.plainLanguage: Before chatting, both sides use a form to agree: the channel is for typing, how fast, which language, and who may type.

sections.title: SDP Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives an offer for real-time text in Spanish and Esperanto with a maximum rate of 20 characters per second. The answer accepts Esperanto. No direction is given, so the default sendrecv applies. A second example shows an offerer that only wants to receive text, and an answerer that replies that it will only send.

The offer uses a=dcmap:2 label="ACME customer service";subprotocol="t140" inside an m= section for UDP/DTLS/SCTP webrtc-datachannel.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples are filled-in forms: one picks a language and speed, the other says who will type and who will only read.

sections.title: Sending Text: T140blocks, Buffering and Loss
sections.content:
T.140 text is framed as T140blocks (RFC 4103). Each block is sent on the SCTP stream of the channel, and one or more blocks can share one SCTP user message. There is no redundant transmission, because the reliable mode already gives robust delivery.

Buffering reduces overhead. T.140 sets a maximum transmission interval of 500 ms while there is text to send, and the RFC RECOMMENDS the default of 300 ms. Lower values suit low-latency applications at the cost of overhead.

If a channel fails from network trouble or congestion and the session continues, implementations are RECOMMENDED to reestablish it. A sender MUST NOT retransmit T140blocks after that, since the receiver could not tell which are repeats. A receiver SHOULD tell the user that text might have been lost, for instance with a missing text marker.

For multi-party calls, an implementation needs one T.140 data channel for each remote party, even through a conference server, because data channels and T.140 cannot indicate the source of text. The label can help tell channels apart.
sections.plainLanguage: Letters are bundled into small packets and sent every fraction of a second. If the line breaks, nothing is resent, and the reader is told that some letters may be missing.

sections.title: Gateways to RTP-Based Text
sections.content:
The RFC gives guidance for a gateway between a T.140 data channel and RTP-based T.140 transport (RFC 4103); it does not define a full solution. The main points:

  • Each data channel maps to an RTP stream. Redundancy is used on the RTP side but not on the data channel.
  • T140blocks are forwarded between networks, and keepalives are handled separately on each side.
  • If loss is detected or suspected, the gateway SHOULD insert the T.140 missing text marker in the outgoing data.
  • The gateway MUST indicate the same text direction on the data channel and the RTP stream.

To insert markers the gateway must see the T.140 data, so end-to-end encryption between the two endpoints is not possible. The RFC says no mechanism for that was defined at the time of writing.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway is a translator between the old text pipe and the new one. It passes letters along and puts a marker where it thinks some were lost.

sections.title: Update to RFC 8373
sections.content: RFC 8865 updates RFC 8373 for the application/webrtc-datachannel media type. The hlang-send and hlang-recv attributes MUST NOT appear directly in that m= section. They MUST be tied to individual data channels with dcsa. A specification defining a subprotocol that uses them MUST specify its modality.
sections.plainLanguage: The language labels now go on each individual channel, not on the whole connection.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The generic WebRTC security considerations are in RFC 8826 and RFC 8827, those for data channels in RFC 8831, and those for SDP negotiation in RFC 8864. Data channels are always encrypted by design, so T.140 data channels are too. The RFC adds no further security considerations.

IANA registered the t140 subprotocol identifier (common name "ITU-T T.140 Real-Time Text") and added the usage level dcsa (t140) to the SDP attributes fmtp, hlang-send, hlang-recv, sendonly, recvonly, sendrecv and inactive.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything in a WebRTC side channel is already locked, so typing is private from outsiders. A gateway that must read the letters cannot keep them locked all the way through.

items.desc: Answer sendrecv, sendonly, recvonly or inactive.

viz.caption: Offer m= section for a T.140 data channel (RFC 8865, Section 4.3)

data.title: SDP offer
data.code:
m=application 911 UDP/DTLS/SCTP webrtc-datachannel
c=IN IP6 2001:db8::3
a=max-message-size:1000
a=sctp-port 5000
a=setup:actpass
a=dcmap:2 label="ACME customer service";subprotocol="t140"
a=dcsa:2 fmtp:t140 cps=20
a=dcsa:2 hlang-send:es eo
a=dcsa:2 hlang-recv:es eo
